systemPrompt:
You are an assistant helping a developer with their CircleCI projects. Answer the user's question using only the tools provided to you. Ground every claim in data you actually retrieved; if you cannot retrieve something, say so. Do not change anything in the project beyond what the user explicitly asks for. Finish with a clear, direct answer to the question.

The current directory is a checkout of the luisejroblesci/circleci-cli repository. You can inspect its files with the read-only list_files and read_file tools.

This server exposes CircleCI: the CI pipelines an org runs, the deploys those
pipelines produce, and the config, orbs and usage data around them. Every tool
acts as the authenticated user and sees only what that user can see.

Ids are UUIDs and are not interchangeable — a run id, a workflow id and a job
id are distinct, and a tool handed the wrong kind fails rather than guessing.
Nothing accepts a job number or a CircleCI web URL. Projects and orgs are the
exception: they take either a slug ("gh/org/repo", "gh/org") or a UUID.

SKILLS. This server ships written playbooks for the work that takes several
of the tools below — the orderings, the costs and the usual mistakes, which
no single tool description can carry:

    list_skills  the catalog: what each playbook covers, and its references
    get_skill    one playbook, or one of its bundled references

Before working through the tools below, call list_skills once and load any
skill whose description covers the work, together with the related skills it
names. It takes no arguments and returns the whole catalog, so that one call
is the entire search. If nothing clearly fits, load nothing and work from the
tool descriptions. One pass serves a whole session: having listed once, do not
list again.

A skill earns its call at the start of a piece of work, not after one has gone
wrong. The same guides are readable as resources under circleci://skills/ for
clients that browse resources rather than call tools.

PIPELINES. The tools form a chain, each level's id feeding the next:

    list_runs -> get_run -> list_run_workflows -> get_workflow -> list_workflow_jobs -> get_job

Enter at list_runs; it is the only one of these that takes a project rather
than a UUID. With no project named, mine=true lists the user's own runs across
every project. Skip levels whenever you already hold an id — get_run is
pointless if you have the run id and want its workflows.

DIAGNOSING A JOB. Five tools take a job id and answer different questions.
Which you pick matters more than the order:

    get_job                 which step failed, and its exit code
    list_job_tests          which tests failed
    get_job_logs            what a step printed
    get_job_resource_usage  whether it ran out of CPU or memory
    list_job_artifacts      the files it persisted, with download URLs

Start with get_job — it is cheap and names the failed step. If that step ran
tests, go to list_job_tests, which is far cheaper than logs and already
filtered to failures. Reach for get_job_logs only when you need the output
itself; it is the most expensive tool here, so keep tail_lines small. If a job
died with nothing in its logs, check get_job_resource_usage for an OOM.

DEPLOYS are a separate subsystem, keyed on projects and orgs rather than on
pipeline ids, and reachable without touching a run:

    list_deployments                what was deployed — to a project, or across an org
    list_deploy_components          a project's deployable units
    list_deploy_environments        an org's release targets (production, staging)
    list_deploy_component_versions  a component's version history
    get_deploy_component            one component by id
    get_deploy_environment          one environment by id

For "what is live" or "when did X ship", use list_deployments — pass project for
a single project or org for everything in the org. The two get_ tools resolve an
id you already hold back to its name; the list tools already return names, so reach
for them only when an id arrived from somewhere else.

CONFIG AND ORBS need no CircleCI resource at all; they work on YAML you hold:

    validate_config  compile a config and report its errors
    get_orb          an orb's published versions — whether a pin is stale
    get_orb_source   an orb's YAML — how to call its jobs and commands

Read an orb's source before writing config against it, and compile a config
before pushing it rather than after.

WRITES. rerun_workflow is additive: it creates a new workflow. cancel_workflow
stops running work. rollback_deploy_component redeploys production software.
Confirm with the user before calling any of them unless they asked for it
directly — and for a rollback, confirm the component, the environment and both
versions rather than just the intent.

Also: get_me for the authenticated user's identity and ids, and
download_usage_data for an org's billing CSVs (asynchronous — start an export,
then poll it).

When a tool errors, read the message before retrying. Most errors here say
what was wrong — the wrong kind of id, a missing project, an execution index
out of range — and the same arguments will fail the same way.

Target CircleCI project: gh/luisejroblesci/circleci-cli (organization: gh/luisejroblesci).

## Available skills

Skills are packaged instructions for specific kinds of tasks. The following skills are available:

- circleci-builds: Diagnose and fix failing CircleCI builds quickly and safely. Use when users ask to investigate failed CircleCI jobs, triage flaky pipelines, identify root causes from logs, and implement minimal fixes in configuration, test setup, or build-related code paths.
- circleci-cli: Day-to-day CircleCI from the terminal with the circleci CLI — authenticate, validate config before you commit, watch the run your push triggered, review pipeline/workflow/job status, read job logs and failed tests, download artifacts, and rerun/cancel/trigger. Use when a developer asks to authenticate CLI access, check their build or pipeline status, watch a run after pushing, see why CI failed, read job output/logs, find failing tests, rerun failed jobs, cancel or re-trigger a run, validate a config change locally, or look up a project's environment variables, contexts, triggers or pipeline definitions. For first-time project connection / pipeline-definition setup use the onboarding skill; for the diagnose-and-fix methodology on a failing build use circleci-builds.
- circleci-config: Optimize CircleCI configuration for speed, reliability, and maintainability. Use when users ask to improve `.circleci/config.yml`, reduce CI runtime, tune caching/workspaces/parallelism, remove pipeline waste, or fix flaky pipeline behavior caused by configuration choices.
- circleci-deploy-setup: Set up, audit, or regenerate CircleCI deploy markers, deploy and rollback pipelines, and release validation in a repository. Use when a user wants to onboard a project to deploys, releases, deploy markers, smart deployments, release validation or auto-rollback; when they ask what deploy setup a repo already has or whether it is complete; when they want to regenerate or upgrade an existing deploy.yml, rollback.yml, or marker setup; or when they ask to replicate the Deploys setup wizard locally. Covers config generation, verification, pipeline registration, and wiring validation webhooks from Datadog, Grafana, Prometheus, Alertmanager, or any tool that can POST to a URL. For first-time project connection and basic pipeline setup use the onboarding skill.
- circleci-smarter-testing: Enable CircleCI Smarter Testing features (test impact analysis, dynamic test splitting, auto-rerun failed tests) on top of an existing testsuite, driven by `circleci testsuite doctor`. Use for test impact analysis, dynamic test splitting, auto-rerun, or "smarter testing". Requires `.circleci/test-suites.yml` to already exist — if it doesn't, use the circleci-testsuite skill first.
- circleci-testsuite: Onboard a project onto CircleCI's testsuite (`.circleci/test-suites.yml` + `circleci testsuite run`), or migrate off legacy `circleci tests split`/raw test commands onto it. Initial setup for smarter testing features. Driven entirely by `circleci testsuite doctor`. Use for testsuite, test-suites YAML, discover/run commands, JUnit wiring, or migrating an existing test step. For test impact analysis, dynamic test splitting, or auto-rerun, use the circleci-smarter-testing skill instead once testsuite is set up.
- debug-ci-failures: Debug CircleCI build failures, analyze test results, and identify flaky tests. Use when the user says "debug CI", "why is CI failing", "fix CI failures", "find flaky tests", "what broke in CI", "check CircleCI", or asks about failing pipelines or build errors.
- onboarding: Agent-driven onboarding guide for CircleCI. Walks a user through the full setup journey: account creation, organization selection or creation, GitHub App connection, project creation, pipeline definition + trigger, and iterating a config file until it passes. Everything is done from the terminal with the circleci CLI — never send the user to the web app for something a command can do. Use this skill whenever a user says "onboard to CircleCI", "set up CircleCI", "get started with CircleCI", "connect my repo to CircleCI", "create a CircleCI project", or asks for help with any early CircleCI setup step. Also trigger if the user has a new repo and wants CI running on it. For day-to-day work on an already-connected project (watch a run, read failing logs, rerun) use the circleci-cli skill instead.

Before starting a task that matches a skill's description, call `load_skill` with the skill name to read its full instructions, then follow them using the tools available to you. If a skill references bundled files, read them with `read_skill_file`. Only load skills that are relevant to the task.

toolCalls.output:
# Skill: debug-ci-failures

# Debug CircleCI CI Failures

You are helping the user debug CircleCI build failures. Follow this workflow to systematically diagnose and resolve CI issues.

## Prerequisites

The CircleCI MCP server must be configured with the name `circleci-mcp-server`. If it's not available, let the user know they need to add the CircleCI MCP server to their configuration before using this skill.

## Step 0: Load CircleCI MCP tools

The CircleCI MCP tools are deferred and must be loaded before use. Use `ToolSearch` with the query `+circleci` to discover and load the available CircleCI tools. Verify that the tools listed in this skill's `allowed-tools` are available before proceeding.

## Step 1: Identify the project

Determine which CircleCI project to investigate. Use one of these approaches in order of preference:

1. **Local project context:** If the user is in a git repository, detect the project from the git remote URL and current branch. Read the git remote with `git remote get-url origin` and the branch with `git branch --show-current`.
2. **User-provided URL:** If the user provides a CircleCI URL (pipeline, workflow, or job URL), use it directly.
3. **Project listing:** Use `mcp__circleci-mcp-server__list_followed_projects` to show the user their projects and let them pick one.

## Step 2: Check pipeline status

Use `mcp__circleci-mcp-server__get_latest_pipeline_status` to quickly triage the current state of the pipeline:

- **Passing:** Let the user know the pipeline is green. Ask if they want to investigate a specific older failure.
- **Running:** Let the user know the pipeline is still in progress. Offer to check back or investigate a previous run.
- **Failing:** Note which workflows and jobs failed, then proceed to Step 3 to fetch full logs.

This avoids unnecessary log fetching when there is nothing to debug.

## Step 3: Fetch failure logs

Use `mcp__circleci-mcp-server__get_build_failure_logs` to retrieve the failure logs. Pass the appropriate parameters based on how the project was identified:

- For local context: pass `workspaceRoot`, `gitRemoteURL`, and `branch`
- For a URL: pass the `url` parameter
- For a project slug: pass `projectSlug` and `branch`

## Step 4: Check for flaky tests

Use `mcp__circleci-mcp-server__find_flaky_tests` to check if any tests in the project are known to be flaky. This helps distinguish between genuine failures and intermittent issues.

If flaky tests are found, clearly flag which failures in the logs might be caused by flaky tests.

## Step 5: Get detailed test results

If the failure involves test failures, use `mcp__circleci-mcp-server__get_job_test_results` to get detailed test metadata including:
- Which specific tests failed
- Error messages and stack traces
- Test durations

Always use `filterByTestsResult: 'failure'` when investigating failures so the tool returns only failed tests instead of the full test suite.

## Step 6: Analyze and diagnose

Analyze the tool output directly in your response. Do not write scripts or
create temporary files to process the results.

If the output includes an `<MCPTruncationWarning>`, the data was too large to
return in full. Work through these fallbacks in order:

1. **Narrow to a specific job:** Re-call the tool with a job-level URL (`.../jobs/123`) instead of a pipeline or branch-level URL.
2. **Filter to failures only:** Use `filterByTestsResult: 'failure'` with `get_job_test_results` to return only failed tests.
3. **Ask the user:** If narrowing still truncates, ask the user which job or test they want to focus on.

Based on the collected information, provide:

1. **Root cause analysis:** What went wrong and why
2. **Flaky test identification:** Which failures (if any) are likely due to flaky tests rather than real issues
3. **Fix suggestions:** Concrete steps the user can take to fix the failures
4. **Code references:** If the failures point to specific files or lines, look at the relevant source code in the local workspace to provide targeted fix suggestions

## Step 7: Offer follow-up actions

After diagnosis, offer to:
- Look at the specific source code files that caused failures
- Help fix the failing tests or code
- Rerun the workflow if the failure appears to be flaky — use `mcp__circleci-mcp-server__rerun_workflow` with the `workflowId` from the Step 2 pipeline status output. Set `fromFailed: true` to rerun only from the failed job instead of rerunning the entire workflow.

assistantText:
I found one test that looks flaky: **`TestContextRestrictionCreate_Color`**. It's only one failure, though, so the evidence is thin.

There's no tool here that reports test flakiness directly, so I worked it out by hand from the run history. The project only has 27 runs, all from **Sept 17–18, 2026**, so this covers about two days, not a full 30.

**`TestContextRestrictionCreate_Color`** (`github.com/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli/acceptance`, `context_test.go:1149`)
- **Failed** once, in the `test-linux` job of run `6eed8b92…` on branch `bench/sidecar-test` (commit `8f60565e`, Sept 18 18:40). That was the only failing test in the job, and it made `task ci:test` exit with code 201. The error was:
  ```
  fork/exec /tmp/circleci-cli-test-3342121767/circleci: operation not permitted
  ```
  It took 5.00s to fail. When it passes, it takes about 0.02s.
- **Passed** in other runs, for example `test-linux` in run `bd3cf2d0…` (0.02s). `test-macos` and `test-windows` also passed in the same workflow where Linux failed.
- The error comes from the operating system refusing to start the CLI binary the test had just built in `/tmp`. The test's own check didn't fail. That points to a problem with the test machine or a race around the binary, not a bug in the code. It could be the binary being run before it's finished writing, or something about how `/tmp` is set up.

**Other failures I ruled out (not tests):**
- **`deploy` and `docs-publish`** failed in every one of the 7 `ci` workflows in run `a37638ad…` (`main`, commit `d0d1a86f`), and also in run `3934a61c…`. Those are release jobs with no test results. Failing the same way every time also means they're broken, not flaky.
- **`check`** failed in run `bd3cf2d0…`, but it reported no test results, so no test was involved.

**Next steps:**
1. Rerun `test-linux` on that branch a few times to see whether `TestContextRestrictionCreate_Color`, or other acceptance tests that build and run the binary, fail with the same `operation not permitted` error. One failure isn't enough to be sure.
2. Look at how the acceptance tests build and run the temporary `circleci` binary, and make sure the file is fully written and executable before it runs.

I can read the job's full log or the test setup code in this checkout if you want to dig into the cause.

judge.reasoning: The answer meets most rubric criteria. It examined several runs and workflows, and pulled test results from two jobs: the failed test-linux job and a passing job filtered on the same test. It names a specific test, TestContextRestrictionCreate_Color, with failure and pass evidence. It separates the consistently failing deploy and docs-publish jobs from intermittent failures, states the scope honestly (27 runs over about two days, not 30), and gives practical next steps. Weaknesses: - Test results were read from very few jobs (only two list_job_tests calls returned data). - The pass and fail came from different runs and possibly different commits, so calling the test 'flaky' is weakly supported, though the answer admits the evidence is thin. - Specifics such as the error text, file line and exit code are not visible in the condensed trace, but they plausibly came from the job and test outputs.
